name: Faildergdóit
summary:
Faildergdóit, son of Muinemón, was a High King of Ireland according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition. He succeeded to the throne on the death of his father and is said to have been the first king in Ireland whose subjects wore gold rings on their hands. His reign lasted for ten years before being cut short by either Sírna mac Déin or his successor Ollom Fotla, whose father Fíachu Fínscothach had been killed by Failderdóit's father Muinemón. The chronology of Geoffrey Keating's For Finnian is not entirely clear on the circumstances of his death.

Faildergdóit's rule was significant because he implemented a system of taxation that helped to stabilize Ireland's economy during a time of great instability. His successor, Ollom Fotla, continued this policy, and it had a lasting impact on Irish history.

The legacy of Faildergdóit can be seen in the many place names and surnames that bear his name throughout Ireland.

Faildergdóit's life was marked by violence and conflict, particularly with neighboring tribes and kingdoms. His death at the hands of either Sírna mac Déin or Ollom Fotla marked the beginning of a period of instability in Ireland.
